readings.title: Mrs. Rachel at her window (Anne of Green Gables, chapter i, first part)
readings.challenge: Read long, winding sentences and enjoy how the narrator teases a character while describing her.
readings.focus: The novel opens on a neighbour who notices everything and a mystery she cannot solve.
readings.context: L. M. Montgomery’s Anne of Green Gables (1908) is set in Avonlea, an invented farming village on Prince Edward Island in eastern Canada. These first two chapters come before the school-year nights, which begin with Marilla’s surprise in chapter III. Alders and ladies’ eardrops are plants; a buggy is a light carriage and a sorrel mare a reddish-brown horse; Carmody is a nearby village; Lombardies are tall, narrow poplar trees.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, “Mrs. Rachel Lynde Is Surprised,” from the opening to Mrs. Rachel’s survey of the Green Gables supper table; opens “Mrs. Rachel Lynde lived just where the Avonlea main road dipped down into a little…”; closes “…getting fairly dizzy with this unusual mystery about quiet, unmysterious Green Gables.”.

questions.prompt: The first sentence ends with a brook behaving itself as it passes Mrs. Rachel’s door. What does this joke tell you about her before she says a word?
facilitatorNotes: Even the wild brook becomes “quiet, well-conducted” near her house, as if it knows she is watching. The joke shows her as the village’s self-appointed inspector of “decency and decorum.” The next paragraph adds that she is capable and hard-working, so the narrator teases her without making her merely a busybody.
evidence: not even a brook could run past Mrs. Rachel Lynde’s door without due regard for decency and decorum

questions.prompt: How does Mrs. Rachel reason from what she sees of Matthew? Why can she still not solve the mystery?
facilitatorNotes: White collar and best suit mean he is leaving Avonlea; the buggy and mare mean a long way; slow driving means not a doctor. She reasons like a detective, but Matthew is so shy and so rarely goes anywhere that none of her usual explanations fit. The supper table with three plates and everyday dishes only deepens the puzzle.
evidence: he wore a white collar and his best suit of clothes, which was plain proof that he was going out of Avonlea
he wasn’t driving fast enough to be going for a doctor

questions.prompt: What do the Green Gables yard and kitchen suggest about Marilla before we meet her properly? What might the house be missing?
facilitatorNotes: Everything is neat, precise and “painfully clean,” and the kitchen looks like an unused parlour. Marilla distrusts sunshine as “too dancing and irresponsible” for a serious world. The house is orderly but lacks warmth or play; readers can predict what kind of change an unexpected arrival might bring.
evidence: so painfully clean as to give it something of the appearance of an unused parlour
always slightly distrustful of sunshine, which seemed to her too dancing and irresponsible a thing for a world which was meant to be taken seriously

readings.title: A boy from the asylum (Anne of Green Gables, chapter i, second part)
readings.challenge: Weigh two characters’ arguments and notice what each reveals without meaning to.
readings.focus: Marilla explains why she and Matthew are adopting a boy, and Mrs. Rachel predicts disaster.
readings.context: Mrs. Rachel Lynde, who watches the road from her kitchen window, has seen shy Matthew Cuthbert drive off in his best suit and has walked up to Green Gables to ask his sister Marilla why. An orphan asylum was an orphanage; Nova Scotia is a province across the water from the Island. Barnardo homes in England sent poor and orphaned children to Canada as farm workers (Marilla spells the name “Barnado”). Job’s comforters, from the Bible, are friends who make a person feel worse while claiming to help. Strychnine is a poison.
readings.contentNote: Marilla dismisses “stupid, half-grown little French boys” and “London street Arabs,” prejudices against French-speaking Acadians and poor city children common in her time and place. Mrs. Rachel repeats newspaper stories of adopted children setting fires and poisoning a family.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, “Mrs. Rachel Lynde Is Surprised,” from Marilla’s greeting to the end of the chapter; opens ““Good evening, Rachel,” Marilla said briskly. “This is a real fine evening, isn’t it?…”; closes “…station at that very moment her pity would have been still deeper and more profound.”.

questions.prompt: The narrator says Marilla has “a saving something about her mouth” that might have been a sense of humour. Where in this conversation do you see it?
facilitatorNotes: Her lips twitch because she expected Mrs. Rachel’s visit. She answers the shocking news “as if getting boys from orphan asylums in Nova Scotia were part of the usual spring work,” and replies to the poisoning story that they are not getting a girl. Readers may decide the humour is dry and hidden, which matters for how she will treat a child.
evidence: Marilla’s lips twitched understandingly.
as if poisoning wells were a purely feminine accomplishment

questions.prompt: Why did the Cuthberts decide to take a boy? What practical reasons and what prejudices does Marilla’s explanation contain?
facilitatorNotes: Matthew is sixty with a weak heart, and hired help is scarce, so they want a boy old enough to do chores. She also rejects “French boys” and English street children and wants “a born Canadian,” because he “can’t be much different from ourselves.” Students should name the prejudice plainly while noticing that she also promises “a good home and schooling.”
evidence: Matthew is getting up in years, you know—he’s sixty—and he isn’t so spry as he once was.
Give me a native born at least.

questions.prompt: What kind of evidence does Mrs. Rachel offer against adoption, and how does Marilla answer it?
facilitatorNotes: She offers frightening stories from newspapers and hearsay: a fire set on purpose, eggs sucked, a well poisoned. Marilla admits “qualms” but answers that there are risks even in having your own children. A single dramatic story is weak evidence about orphans in general, and Marilla seems to know it.
evidence: Why, it was only last week I read in the paper
There’s risks in people’s having children of their own if it comes to that

questions.prompt: At the end Mrs. Rachel pities the orphan. What does she fear for the child, and what does the narrator’s last sentence add?
facilitatorNotes: She thinks the Cuthberts know nothing about children and will expect a child to act like an adult. The narrator then tells us that the child already waiting at the station would make her pity “still deeper,” a hint that the orphan is not what anyone expects. The chapter ends on a surprise held back for the next.
evidence: they’ll expect him to be wiser and steadier than his own grandfather
her pity would have been still deeper and more profound

readings.title: The girl on the shingles (Anne of Green Gables, chapter ii, first part)
readings.challenge: Compare a narrator’s portrait of a character with what another character can see.
readings.focus: Matthew finds a girl instead of a boy at the station and cannot bring himself to tell her.
readings.context: Mrs. Rachel has learned that Matthew and Marilla Cuthbert, an elderly brother and sister, are adopting an orphan boy to help on their farm, and that Matthew has driven to the Bright River station to meet him. Shingles are thin wooden roof tiles, here stacked on the platform; wincey is a cheap, rough cloth; a carpet-bag is a travelling bag made of carpet.

excerpt.locator: Chapter II, “Matthew Cuthbert Is Surprised,” from the drive to Bright River through Matthew’s decision to take the child home; opens “Matthew Cuthbert and the sorrel mare jogged comfortably over the eight miles to Bright…”; closes “…was late,” he said shyly. “Come along. The horse is over in the yard. Give me your bag.””.

questions.prompt: Before Matthew speaks to the girl, the station-master reports what she said. What does “more scope for imagination” suggest about her?
facilitatorNotes: She would rather sit on a pile of shingles, waiting, than in a closed room, because outside she can imagine more. The phrase sounds like a book, not a child, which amuses the station-master. It prepares us for a character who lives partly in what she imagines.
evidence: ‘There was more scope for imagination,’ she said.

questions.prompt: The narrator describes the girl twice, as an “ordinary observer” and an “extraordinary observer” would. What does the second description add, and why does Matthew see neither?
facilitatorNotes: The ordinary observer sees a thin, freckled child in an ugly dress with red braids; the extraordinary one notices spirit in her eyes, an expressive mouth and a strong chin, and concludes that “no commonplace soul” is there. Matthew is too frightened of girls even to look. The double portrait lets the reader know more than Matthew does.
evidence: an ordinary observer would have seen this
no commonplace soul inhabited the body of this stray woman-child

questions.prompt: Why does Matthew decide “then and there” to take her home instead of explaining the mistake?
facilitatorNotes: She has been afraid he would not come and had planned to sleep in a wild cherry-tree; her glowing eyes and trust make it impossible for him to say she is not wanted. He also cannot leave a child at the station. Readers may see kindness, cowardice about an awkward talk, or both; he plans to “let Marilla do that.”
evidence: He could not tell this child with the glowing eyes that there had been a mistake
it would be lovely to sleep in a wild cherry-tree all white with bloom in the moonshine

readings.title: Talking all the way (Anne of Green Gables, chapter ii, second part)
readings.challenge: Find the serious facts hidden inside a long, cheerful, rambling speech.
readings.focus: On the drive home the girl talks about the orphanage, her imagination and her red hair, and Matthew finds he likes it.
readings.context: At the Bright River station Matthew found a red-haired girl of about eleven instead of the boy he expected. Too shy to tell her of the mistake, he is driving her home to Green Gables and will leave the explaining to Marilla. A belted earl is a high-ranking nobleman; Charlottetown is the Island’s capital; alabaster is smooth white stone.

excerpt.locator: Chapter II, “Matthew Cuthbert Is Surprised,” from the carpet-bag to the girl’s sudden cry of “Mr. Cuthbert”; opens ““Oh, I can carry it,” the child responded cheerfully. “It isn’t heavy. I’ve got all my…”; closes “…good. Mrs. Spencer says—oh, Mr. Cuthbert! Oh, Mr. Cuthbert!! Oh, Mr. Cuthbert!!!””.

questions.prompt: In the middle of her cheerful talk the girl says, “I’ve never belonged to anybody—not really.” Find another moment that shows what her life has been like. Why does she mention these things so lightly?
facilitatorNotes: She describes the asylum as “worse than anything you could imagine,” the donated wincey that all orphans wore, and the asylum trees that “looked like orphans themselves.” Saying it quickly and cheerfully may be how she copes; the reader notices what she hurries past.
evidence: I’ve never belonged to anybody—not really.
They just looked like orphans themselves, those trees did.

questions.prompt: How does she use imagination to deal with things she cannot change? What is the one thing she cannot imagine away?
facilitatorNotes: On the train she imagined a pale blue silk dress instead of the wincey; she chooses to believe the merchant gave the cloth from kindness. But red hair defeats her: she always knows it is “just plain red.” Imagination is a tool for survival, and also has limits she admits.
evidence: because when you _are_ imagining you might as well imagine something worth while
But I _cannot_ imagine that red hair away.

questions.prompt: Matthew answers “Well now, I dunno” again and again. Why does a man who dreads women and girls enjoy this one?
facilitatorNotes: He likes talkative people who do not expect him to talk back, and she is unlike the Avonlea girls who sidle past him timidly. His few words are honest and kind (“you can talk as much as you like”). The chapter suggests an unlikely friendship is beginning.
evidence: Like most quiet folks he liked talkative people when they were willing to do the talking themselves
Oh, you can talk as much as you like. I don’t mind.

readings.title: The White Way of Delight (Anne of Green Gables, chapter ii, end)
readings.challenge: Notice how descriptions of places carry a character’s feelings, and feel the irony when the reader knows more than she does.
readings.focus: The girl names the places she loves and recognises Green Gables as home, while Matthew dreads what must come.
readings.context: Driving from the station, the girl has talked almost without stopping: about the orphanage, about imagining a silk dress instead of her ugly one, and about her red hair. Matthew, to his surprise, has enjoyed it. He has still not told her that he and Marilla meant to adopt a boy. A rose window is a round stained-glass window in a church; Diana was a Roman goddess, which is why Matthew thinks the name “heathenish.”

excerpt.locator: Chapter II, “Matthew Cuthbert Is Surprised,” from the Avenue to the end of the chapter; opens “That was not what Mrs. Spencer had said; neither had the child tumbled out of the buggy…”; closes “…the carpet-bag which contained “all her worldly goods,” she followed him into the house.”.

questions.prompt: The girl can talk without stopping, but the Avenue strikes her silent. Why does she reject the word “pretty” for it?
facilitatorNotes: It is “the first thing I ever saw that couldn’t be improved upon by imagination,” so ordinary words like pretty or beautiful “don’t go far enough.” Her silence lasts three miles, as energetic as her talk. The “queer funny ache” is a feeling of beauty mixed with longing that she will name again when she thinks of home.
evidence: It’s the first thing I ever saw that couldn’t be improved upon by imagination.
Oh, _pretty_ doesn’t seem the right word to use.

questions.prompt: Why does she rename the Avenue and Barry’s pond? What does Matthew’s “thrill” about cucumber grubs add to the scene?
facilitatorNotes: She renames places whose names have “no meaning” to her, and knows a name is right when it gives her a thrill. Matthew honestly offers the only thrill he knows, at ugly grubs; the contrast is funny and gentle, and she politely doubts it is the same kind. It shows two very different minds getting along.
evidence: When I hit on a name that suits exactly it gives me a thrill.
It always kind of gives me a thrill to see them ugly white grubs that spade up in the cucumber beds.

questions.prompt: She guesses which house is Green Gables and says she “felt it was home.” Why does this make the chapter’s ending painful, and why does Matthew compare telling her to killing a lamb?
facilitatorNotes: The reader knows she is not wanted there, so her certainty is dramatic irony. Matthew now thinks only of her disappointment, not of the trouble to himself, and feels he will help to murder “something,” her hope. The last image of her clutching “all her worldly goods” keeps her small and unprotected as she walks in.
evidence: But just as soon as I saw it I felt it was home.
he had an uncomfortable feeling that he was going to assist at murdering something

readings.title: Plain Marilla (Anne of Green Gables, chapter viii, first part)
readings.challenge: Read a character’s strict words and look for signs of feelings she will not show.
readings.focus: Marilla tells Anne she may stay, and the two disagree about names, imagination and prayer.
readings.context: Anne Shirley, the orphan sent by mistake to Matthew and Marilla Cuthbert, has spent a day at Green Gables. After some thought Marilla has decided to keep her but has not yet told her. The night before, Anne said her first prayer ever, asking to be allowed to stay. A fortnight is two weeks; a chromo is a cheap colour print; to scald a dish-cloth is to wash it in boiling water.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VIII, “Anne’s Bringing-up Is Begun,” from the opening through Anne’s first study of the Lord’s Prayer; opens “For reasons best known to herself, Marilla did not tell Anne that she was to stay at…”; closes “…a soft kiss on a pink-cupped bud, and then studied diligently for some moments longer.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Marilla send Anne back to scald the dish-cloth before answering her? What do the conditions in her answer show?
facilitatorNotes: She will not let feeling interrupt a task, and perhaps she is testing Anne or hiding her own softness; the narrator says only “for reasons best known to herself.” She keeps Anne “if you will try to be a good little girl and show yourself grateful,” a cautious, conditional welcome. Anne answers with tears she cannot explain.
evidence: “You haven’t scalded the dish-cloth in clean hot water as I told you to do,” said Marilla immovably.
if you will try to be a good little girl and show yourself grateful

questions.prompt: Anne asks to call her “Aunt Marilla.” What does each of them want, and how do they differ about imagination?
facilitatorNotes: Anne wants to feel she belongs to a family; Marilla refuses to call people “names that don’t belong to them” and believes God does not mean us to imagine our circumstances away. Anne’s “how much you miss!” turns the argument around. Readers may sympathise with either: Marilla’s honesty or Anne’s longing.
evidence: It would make me feel as if I really belonged to you.
Oh, Miss—Marilla, how much you miss!

questions.prompt: Why does Anne imagine herself as the girl in the blue dress in the picture? Is Marilla right to call her words irreverent?
facilitatorNotes: The child stands apart “as if she didn’t belong to anybody, like me,” hoping to be noticed, as Anne hoped when she asked to stay. Marilla thinks such familiar talk about Christ is irreverent, yet she wonders why she did not interrupt sooner, a sign she was listening. Anne’s feeling seems sincere; readers can discuss whether reverence depends on manner or on feeling.
evidence: standing off by herself in the corner as if she didn’t belong to anybody, like me
wondering why she had not broken into this speech long before

readings.title: Katie Maurice and Violetta (Anne of Green Gables, chapter viii, end)
readings.challenge: Read a happy-sounding memory for what it reveals about a lonely past.
readings.focus: Anne hopes for a real friend, remembers two imaginary ones, and decides who she is in front of a mirror.
readings.context: Marilla has told Anne she may stay at Green Gables, refused to be called “Aunt Marilla,” and set her to learn the Lord’s Prayer after scolding her for daydreaming before a picture. A bosom friend is a closest friend; a kindred spirit is someone who thinks and feels as you do. The Duchess in Lewis Carroll’s Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland finds a moral in everything. The Snow Queen is Anne’s name for the cherry tree outside her window.
readings.contentNote: Anne mentions in passing that the man of a family she lived with smashed a glass door while drunk.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VIII, “Anne’s Bringing-up Is Begun,” from Anne’s question about a bosom friend to the end of the chapter; opens ““Marilla,” she demanded presently, “do you think that I shall ever have a bosom friend in…”; closes “…and then, with her chin in her hands, drifted luxuriously out on a sea of day-dreams.”.

questions.prompt: What does Marilla’s remark about Diana show, and how does the narrator’s comparison with the Duchess in Wonderland comment on it?
facilitatorNotes: Marilla adds that being “good and smart” is better than being pretty, because she believes every remark to a child should carry a moral. The comparison with Carroll’s absurd Duchess gently mocks the habit, and Anne simply ignores the moral and seizes on Diana’s prettiness.
evidence: And she is good and smart, which is better than being pretty.
Marilla was as fond of morals as the Duchess in Wonderland

questions.prompt: Anne tells the story of Katie Maurice and Violetta happily. What do these imaginary friends reveal about her life before Green Gables?
facilitatorNotes: She had no real friends, moved from one household to another, and talked to her own reflection in a glass door and to an echo. Small details show hardship: the bookcase held no books, a door was smashed by a drunken man, and at the asylum she “hadn’t the heart” even to imagine a friend. The cheerful telling makes the loneliness more touching.
evidence: Katie was the comfort and consolation of my life.
I hadn’t the heart to imagine a bosom friend at the asylum

questions.prompt: Alone in her room, why can Anne not believe in the Lady Cordelia Fitzgerald? What does she decide instead?
facilitatorNotes: Every time she imagines the grand lady she sees her own freckled face in the glass. She decides it is “a million times nicer” to be Anne of Green Gables than Anne of nowhere; having a place matters more than an imagined title. Her goodnight to Katie and Violetta shows she will stay loyal to the past even as she hopes for Diana.
evidence: No, it isn’t—I can’t make _that_ seem real.
But it’s a million times nicer to be Anne of Green Gables than Anne of nowhere in particular, isn’t it?

readings.title: The missing brooch (Anne of Green Gables, chapter xiv, part 1 of 2)
readings.challenge: Watch the narrator show you a misunderstanding that one character cannot see.
readings.focus: Marilla’s amethyst brooch is gone, and she is sure Anne has taken it and lied.
readings.context: In L. M. Montgomery’s Anne of Green Gables (1908), Anne Shirley, an orphan of eleven, has come to live with Marilla Cuthbert and her shy brother Matthew at Green Gables, their farm in Avonlea on Prince Edward Island. In the chapter before this one, the Sunday-school picnic was announced. Anne has never been to a picnic, and there is to be ice-cream. On Sunday she admired the amethyst brooch Marilla always wears to church, Marilla’s most treasured possession. Once before, Marilla kept Anne in her room until she agreed to apologise to Mrs. Rachel Lynde for an outburst of temper. The Aid Society is a church women’s group; a bureau is a chest of drawers.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XIV, “Anne’s Confession,” from Marilla’s question about her brooch to the shut door on the evening before the picnic; opens “On the Monday evening before the picnic Marilla came down from her room with a troubled…”; closes “But Marilla had gone out and shut the door.”.

questions.prompt: What exactly does Anne admit, and what does she deny? Follow Marilla’s reasoning: why is she so sure Anne is lying?
facilitatorNotes: Anne admits going into the room and pinning the brooch on; she denies taking it out of the room. Marilla reasons that nobody else has been in the room and the brooch is gone, so Anne must have taken it. Given what she knows, her reasoning is not foolish; what she lacks is a third possibility.
evidence: I took it up and I pinned it on my breast just to see how it would look.
there hasn’t been a soul in that room since she was in it, by her own story, until I went up to-night

questions.prompt: Twice the narrator tells us how Marilla hears Anne, not only what Anne says. Find both places. What do they let the reader know that Marilla does not?
facilitatorNotes: Anne speaks “quickly—pertly, Marilla thought,” and her “so there” is “only intended to emphasize her assertion,” but Marilla takes it as defiance. The narrator lets us see that Marilla is misreading Anne’s manner. That makes the reader more inclined than Marilla to believe Anne, though it does not yet prove her innocent.
evidence: pertly, Marilla thought
Anne’s “so there” was only intended to emphasize her assertion, but Marilla took it as a display of defiance.

questions.prompt: Marilla says she minds the lie more than the loss of the brooch. Why might that be, for someone who has just taken on a child?
facilitatorNotes: She feels “a fearful responsibility”: she must trust a child who lives in her house, and lying seems to her worse than temper. Her worry is about Anne’s character and her own judgment in keeping her. Some readers will add that her pride is hurt, or that she fears Mrs. Rachel was right about Anne all along.
evidence: I declare I feel worse about that than about the brooch.
It’s a fearful responsibility to have a child in your house you can’t trust.

questions.prompt: Marilla decides Anne will stay in her room until she confesses, and the picnic is the next day. What could go wrong with this method if Anne is telling the truth?
facilitatorNotes: If Anne did not take the brooch, she has nothing true to confess, so the only way out of the room, and to the picnic, is to confess something false. Marilla has set up a choice between honesty and the thing Anne wants most. Readers can predict what Anne will do; the next night shows it.
evidence: She’ll stay in her room until she confesses
You’ll not go to picnics nor anywhere else until you’ve confessed, Anne.

readings.title: Anne’s confession (Anne of Green Gables, chapter xiv, part 2 of 2)
readings.challenge: Decide who is responsible when a punishment forces a lie.
readings.focus: Anne confesses to losing the brooch, and Marilla finds it.
readings.context: Recap: Marilla’s amethyst brooch disappeared on the Monday before the Sunday-school picnic. Anne admitted trying it on but insisted she put it back; Marilla, sure she was lying, shut her in her room in the east gable until she confessed, picnic or no picnic. Idlewild is the place where Anne and Diana Barry play; the Lake of Shining Waters is Anne’s name for Barry’s pond. To put one’s hand to the plough and not look back, from the Gospel of Luke, means to finish what one has begun. A bread sponge is dough set to rise overnight; Jerry Buote is the hired boy.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XIV, “Anne’s Confession,” from the morning of the picnic to the end of the chapter; opens “Wednesday morning dawned as bright and fair as if expressly made to order for the picnic.…”; closes “…all right yet. And there’s one thing certain, no house will ever be dull that she’s in.””.

questions.prompt: Anne’s confession is full of vivid detail. Which details make it sound true? Which, looking back, should have made Marilla suspicious?
facilitatorNotes: The bridge, the sunlight and the brooch sinking “all purply-sparkling” sound like something witnessed. But she speaks “as if repeating a lesson,” shows no sorrow, and calls it “the best I can do at confessing,” as if it were a performance. Marilla reads the calm as hardness rather than as a sign the story is invented.
evidence: said Anne, as if repeating a lesson she had learned
all purply-sparkling, and sank forevermore beneath the Lake of Shining Waters
And that’s the best I can do at confessing, Marilla.

questions.prompt: “Neither the shelves nor the porch needed it—but Marilla did.” What does Marilla’s scrubbing show about her that her words to Anne and Matthew do not?
facilitatorNotes: She is upset, perhaps uneasy about her own severity, and works it off with her hands. To Matthew she insists she has “let her off entirely too easy,” but her actions suggest she is not at peace. Readers might also see plain anger in the scrubbing; both readings fit.
evidence: Neither the shelves nor the porch needed it—but Marilla did.
I think I’ve let her off entirely too easy.

questions.prompt: Matthew says “she’s never had any bringing up”; Marilla answers “she’s having it now.” What does each think Anne needs?
facilitatorNotes: Matthew asks for allowances: a child with no upbringing cannot be judged by ordinary rules. Marilla thinks firm correction is exactly what is missing. The chapter later tests her view, since her firmness produced a false confession. Some readers will still side with Marilla’s principle, if not with how she applied it.
evidence: And there should be allowances made, Marilla. You know she’s never had any bringing up.
Well, she’s having it now,

questions.prompt: Marilla says “I drove you to it” but also that the false confession was “very wrong.” Who is more to blame, and does Marilla’s apology settle it?
facilitatorNotes: A defensible answer is that both are: Marilla made confession the only way out, and Anne chose to invent a crime. Marilla admits her share first and asks Anne’s forgiveness before giving hers, which is unusual for an adult in this book. Readers can also argue that Anne’s lie was the natural result of an unjust rule and hardly her fault at all.
evidence: But I drove you to it.
it was very wrong to do so
anyhow I’m responsible for it

readings.title: The way to school (Anne of Green Gables, chapter xv, part 1 of 3)
readings.challenge: Notice how the narrator both shares and gently teases Anne’s view of the world.
readings.focus: Anne and Diana walk to school by the paths Anne has named, and Anne reports on her first day.
readings.context: In L. M. Montgomery’s Anne of Green Gables (1908), the orphan Anne Shirley has been living since June with Marilla and Matthew Cuthbert at Green Gables, in Avonlea on Prince Edward Island. Diana Barry, from the next farm, is her bosom friend. In September Anne starts at the Avonlea school. A “tempest in a teapot” is a great fuss about something small. Queen’s Academy is in Charlottetown, the Island’s capital. The “fourth” and “fifth book” are levels of school reader; a slate is a small framed board pupils wrote on.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XV, “A Tempest in the School Teapot,” from Anne’s “What a splendid day!” through her report on her first day at school; opens ““What a splendid day!” said Anne, drawing a long breath. “Isn’t it good just to be alive…”; closes “…were tripping blithely down the Birch Path, two of the happiest little girls in Avonlea.”.

questions.prompt: Compare Anne’s first speech with Diana’s thoughts about the raspberry tarts. What does each girl notice about the same morning?
facilitatorNotes: Anne feels the whole day and even pities people not yet born for missing it; Diana is working out how many bites ten girls get from three tarts. The narrator enjoys both: Anne’s rapture and Diana’s practical sense. The friendship works partly because they are different.
evidence: I pity the people who aren’t born yet for missing it.
mentally calculating if the three juicy, toothsome, raspberry tarts reposing there were divided among ten girls how many bites each girl would have

questions.prompt: Why does a name matter so much to Anne? Use what she says about Lover’s Lane and about Diana’s “Birch Path.”
facilitatorNotes: Naming lets her imagine more into a place than is there (“We can imagine the lovers into it”), and the lane is somewhere she can think out loud. She dismisses “Birch Path” as a name “anybody” could think of. Readers may find this a little vain, and Anne herself admits “It’s nice to be clever at something.”
evidence: We can imagine the lovers into it, you know.
I like that lane because you can think out loud there without people calling you crazy.
Anybody can think of a name like that.

questions.prompt: After Anne calls the Birch Path “one of the prettiest places in the world,” the narrator begins, “It was.” How does the narrator’s description support Anne, and where does it joke about her?
facilitatorNotes: The narrator agrees and adds sensory detail: light “as flawless as the heart of a diamond,” birches, ferns, bird calls. Then comes a joke: you might see a rabbit if you were quiet, which with Anne and Diana happened “about once in a blue moon.” The narrator loves Anne’s world but is not lost in it.
evidence: It was. Other people besides Anne thought so when they stumbled on it.
which, with Anne and Diana, happened about once in a blue moon

questions.prompt: Anne’s report on her first day mixes gossip, complaint and delight. What does she notice about the master, Mr. Phillips? Is Marilla right to stop her?
facilitatorNotes: She repeats other girls’ stories that he favours Prissy Andrews, and she resents his showing her marked-up slate to the class. Marilla wants respect for teachers and no tale-bearing. Readers can argue either way: Anne is gossiping, but her observations about a master who shames pupils in public may be worth hearing.
evidence: He’s all the time curling his moustache and making eyes at Prissy Andrews.
he held up my slate so that everybody could see it, all marked over
You don’t go to school to criticize the master.

readings.title: “Carrots!” (Anne of Green Gables, chapter xv, part 2 of 3)
readings.challenge: Weigh a punishment against the offence and the provocation.
readings.focus: Gilbert Blythe comes back to school, and Anne meets him in the worst way.
readings.context: Recap: Anne has been three weeks at the Avonlea school, where she sits with her friend Diana Barry. She likes the other girls but not the master, Mr. Phillips, who spends his time with sixteen-year-old Prissy Andrews and who held up Anne’s marked-up slate for the class to see. A “take notice” is a joke notice chalked on a wall to pair a boy’s and a girl’s names. To be “head” of a class is to stand first in a spelling contest; “ebullition” means a boiling up. New Brunswick is the province across the strait from Prince Edward Island, and Alberta is far to the west. “The iron has entered into my soul” is an old phrase from the Psalms for lasting pain.
readings.contentNote: A boy mocks a girl’s red hair; she breaks her slate over his head, and the master shames her in front of the school. Mr. Phillips’s favouritism toward a sixteen-year-old pupil is reported as gossip.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XV, “A Tempest in the School Teapot,” from Diana’s news of Gilbert Blythe to the walk home after school; opens ““I guess Gilbert Blythe will be in school to-day,” said Diana. “He’s been visiting his…”; closes “…if nothing else had happened. But when things begin to happen they are apt to keep on.”.

questions.prompt: Before Anne meets Gilbert, what does she learn about him from Diana? What does Diana’s voice give away about her own feelings?
facilitatorNotes: He is handsome, teases the girls, and is used to being head of his class, though he lost years of school in Alberta. Diana complains that he torments them, but the narrator says she “rather liked” it. Anne answers that she is glad to have real competition, which sets up a rivalry before they have spoken.
evidence: Diana’s voice indicated that she rather liked having her life tormented out than not.
he’s used to being head of his class, I can tell you

questions.prompt: On the walk, Anne says she would “rather be pretty than clever.” How does that help explain why “Carrots!” wounds her more than “crow” wounds Diana?
facilitatorNotes: Anne is sensitive about her freckles and hair and wants above all to be pretty; Diana is admired for her black hair and can laugh at “crow.” Gilbert has hit the place where Anne is weakest, in front of everyone. Readers may add that Gilbert wanted her attention and did not know how much it would hurt.
evidence: I’d rather be pretty than clever.
There’s a great deal of difference between being called a crow and being called carrots,

questions.prompt: Gilbert says at once, “It was my fault.” Why does Mr. Phillips ignore him, and how does the narrator judge the master’s punishment?
facilitatorNotes: Mr. Phillips punishes what he saw, the blow, and does not ask about the cause. The narrator mocks his solemnity (“as if the mere fact of being a pupil of his ought to root out all evil passions”) and the cruelty of reading the words aloud for the youngest pupils. A reader can still hold that Anne deserved some punishment for striking Gilbert; the question is whether this one was just.
evidence: Mr. Phillips paid no heed to Gilbert.
as if the mere fact of being a pupil of his ought to root out all evil passions from the hearts of small imperfect mortals
so that even the primer class, who couldn’t read writing, should understand it

questions.prompt: Gilbert apologises, and Anne will not forgive him. Is she right? What does the chapter’s last sentence suggest about what comes next?
facilitatorNotes: His apology seems sincere (“contritely”), and Diana says he has never apologised before. Anne’s hurt and pride, and her taste for drama (“The iron has entered into my soul”), make forgiveness impossible for now. Readers may sympathise with her or find her unfair. The last sentence promises more trouble: “when things begin to happen they are apt to keep on.”
evidence: I’m awful sorry I made fun of your hair, Anne,
I shall never forgive Gilbert Blythe,
But when things begin to happen they are apt to keep on.

readings.title: Anne leaves school (Anne of Green Gables, chapter xv, part 3 of 3)
readings.challenge: Judge adults’ decisions from what they say to children and what they say to each other.
readings.focus: Singled out for punishment again, Anne refuses to go back to school, and Mrs. Rachel gives advice.
readings.context: Recap: on the day Gilbert Blythe returned to school he held up Anne’s braid and called her “Carrots!”; she cracked her slate over his head. The master, Mr. Phillips, ignored Gilbert’s confession that he had teased her and made Anne stand before the class under the words “Ann Shirley has a very bad temper.” Anne refused Gilbert’s apology and vowed never to forgive him. Spruce gum is the hardened resin of spruce trees, which children chewed. A scapegoat is someone blamed for what many did; a trustee is one of the local men who hire the teacher. Priscilla is Prissy Andrews’s full name.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XV, “A Tempest in the School Teapot,” from the noon hour in Mr. Bell’s spruce grove to the end of the chapter; opens “Avonlea scholars often spent noon hour picking gum in Mr. Bell’s spruce grove over the…”; closes “…pity’s sake borrow it handier home. I should think you had an imagination, sure enough.””.

questions.prompt: Why does Mr. Phillips punish Anne and no one else? What does the narrator mean when he does it “to save his word”?
facilitatorNotes: A dozen pupils were late, but he does not want the bother of punishing them all, so he picks one to show he meant his threat. Anne, who was not even picking gum, arrived last with flowers in her hair and is an easy target. His sarcastic “so fond of the boys’ company” adds insult.
evidence: he didn’t want the bother of punishing a dozen pupils; but it was necessary to do something to save his word, so he looked about for a scapegoat
since you seem to be so fond of the boys’ company we shall indulge your taste for it this afternoon

questions.prompt: While Anne sits beside Gilbert, Mr. Phillips is writing verses “To Priscilla,” and Gilbert slips Anne a candy heart. What does each detail show?
facilitatorNotes: The verses show the master’s mind is on Prissy, not his pupils, so he does not even notice Anne skipping her history class. The candy heart reading “You are sweet” is Gilbert’s peace offering; Anne grinds it to powder in a deliberate, theatrical refusal. Some readers will see Gilbert’s gift as kind, others as more teasing.
evidence: who had been writing some verses “To Priscilla” before he called the class
dropped it on the floor, ground it to powder beneath her heel

questions.prompt: Mrs. Rachel tells Marilla that Mr. Phillips was in the wrong, but “it doesn’t do to say so to the children.” What does she really think of him? Is her advice wise?
facilitatorNotes: She thinks him a bad teacher who keeps poor order, neglects the young pupils and holds his job through his uncle; she also thinks Anne was rightly punished the first day but not the second. Her advice is to let Anne stay home until she cools off. The narrator teases her love of giving advice, yet her reading of Anne proves sound. Readers can question whether adults should hide their judgment of a teacher from children.
evidence: It’s my belief that Mr. Phillips was in the wrong. Of course, it doesn’t do to say so to the children, you know.
Mr. Phillips isn’t any good at all as a teacher.
Mrs. Lynde dearly loved to be asked for advice

questions.prompt: The chapter ends not with Gilbert but with Anne weeping over Diana’s imagined wedding. Why does Marilla laugh? How does this ending connect to the chapter title, “A Tempest in the School Teapot”?
facilitatorNotes: Anne is grieving over something that has not happened and may not for years, and she cries “luxuriously,” half enjoying it. Marilla’s “borrow trouble … handier home” means: if you must worry in advance, worry about something closer. The title names the chapter’s pattern: great storms over small things. Readers may also notice that Marilla laughing so hard is itself rare, which shows how Anne is changing her.
evidence: sobbed Anne luxuriously
if you must borrow trouble, for pity’s sake borrow it handier home
When had he heard Marilla laugh like that before?

readings.title: Diana comes to tea (Anne of Green Gables, chapter xvi, part 1 of 2)
readings.challenge: Notice clues the writer plants that a reader can see and a character cannot.
readings.focus: Marilla lets Anne give her first tea party, and the girls play at being grown-up.
readings.context: In L. M. Montgomery’s Anne of Green Gables (1908), the orphan Anne Shirley lives with Marilla and Matthew Cuthbert at Green Gables in Avonlea, Prince Edward Island. Her bosom friend Diana Barry lives at Orchard Slope, the next farm. After a quarrel with the master, Mr. Phillips, Anne has stopped going to school. The Aid Society is a church women’s group; to let tea “draw” is to let it steep. Preserves that are “beginning to work” are starting to ferment. Raspberry cordial is a sweet, non-alcoholic fruit drink. The Lily Sands is a ship loading potatoes, and an aftermath is a second growth of grass after mowing.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XVI, “Diana Is Invited to Tea with Tragic Results,” from the October opening to Diana’s praise of the raspberry cordial; opens “October was a beautiful month at Green Gables, when the birches in the hollow turned as…”; closes “…than Mrs. Lynde’s although she brags of hers so much. It doesn’t taste a bit like hers.””.

questions.prompt: Why does Marilla hesitate before letting Anne invite Diana? What does Anne look forward to most?
facilitatorNotes: Marilla worries the excitement will make Anne even more forgetful (“more addle-pated than ever”), especially after she forgot the tea last time. Anne looks forward less to the food than to the role: sitting at the head of the table, pouring, asking Diana if she takes sugar when she already knows. She wants to play at being grown-up.
evidence: it may make you more addle-pated than ever
It will seem so nice and grown-uppish.
And asking Diana if she takes sugar! I know she doesn’t but of course I’ll ask her just as if I didn’t know.

questions.prompt: The girls greet each other “as gravely as if they had never met before.” What makes their polite conversation funny, and what breaks it up?
facilitatorNotes: They are copying adult manners, knocking at the front door, shaking hands and asking after health they already know is excellent. The narrator’s asides (“just as if she had not seen Mrs. Barry picking apples”) point up the pretence. It breaks when Anne forgets to be dignified and jumps up to go to the orchard.
evidence: both little girls shook hands as gravely as if they had never met before
just as if she had not seen Mrs. Barry picking apples that morning in excellent health and spirits
said Anne, forgetting to be dignified and jumping up quickly

questions.prompt: Diana’s school news comes in one long sentence. What picture of Avonlea school does it give, and why does it stop where it does?
facilitatorNotes: Rivalries, superstitions, take-notices, a whipping and a father’s threat, a new hood, a quarrel between sisters’ beaus: a small world full of drama, told in Diana’s breathless rhythm. It stops at Gilbert Blythe because Anne will not hear his name, which shows she has not forgiven him. Readers might wonder what Diana was going to say about him.
evidence: and everybody missed Anne so and wished she’d come to school again; and Gilbert Blythe—
But Anne didn’t want to hear about Gilbert Blythe.

questions.prompt: Something may be wrong with the “raspberry cordial.” Which clues has Montgomery planted, and what do you predict?
facilitatorNotes: Marilla said the second shelf of the sitting-room closet, but there is no bottle there and Anne finds one on the top shelf; Anne drinks none; Diana drinks three generous tumblerfuls and says it tastes nothing like Mrs. Lynde’s. A careful reader may suspect the bottle is something else. The chapter title, “with Tragic Results,” adds to the suspicion.
evidence: there was no bottle of raspberry cordial there. Search revealed it away back on the top shelf.
I don’t believe I’ll have any just now.
It doesn’t taste a bit like hers.

readings.title: Tragic results (Anne of Green Gables, chapter xvi, part 2 of 2)
readings.challenge: Follow how one mistake is judged differently by different people.
readings.focus: Diana goes home sick, and Mrs. Barry forbids the friendship.
readings.context: Recap: Marilla let Anne invite Diana to tea while she was out, and told her she might serve the raspberry cordial on the second shelf of the sitting-room closet. Anne found a bottle on the top shelf instead. Diana drank three big tumblerfuls and said it was the nicest she had ever tasted; Anne drank none. Before Green Gables, Anne lived with a Mrs. Thomas, whose husband drank. “Heaping coals of fire on my head,” from the Bible, means being shamed by kindness. Currant wine is wine made from currants; “malice prepense” means deliberate ill will; a suppliant is someone who begs a favour.
readings.contentNote: A child becomes drunk by accident on homemade wine. Anne recalls a drunken man from her past, and Marilla says she would cure a greedy child with “a right good spanking.”

excerpt.locator: Chapter XVI, “Diana Is Invited to Tea with Tragic Results,” from Anne’s story of the cake and the pudding sauce to the end of the chapter; opens ““I should think Marilla’s raspberry cordial would prob’ly be much nicer than Mrs.…”; closes “…child’s tear-stained face. Then she bent down and kissed the flushed cheek on the pillow.”.

questions.prompt: While Anne tells her stories about the cake and the pudding sauce, what is happening to Diana? What is funny, and a little uncomfortable, about the subject of Anne’s stories?
facilitatorNotes: Diana is getting drunk while Anne talks on without looking. Anne’s stories are about her imagination making her forget practical things, the flour and the cover, at the very moment a practical mistake is unfolding in front of her. The reader suspects what Anne cannot see, so the comedy and the dread grow together.
evidence: I’m a great trial to her.
Flour is so essential to cakes, you know.
Diana had stood up very unsteadily; then she sat down again, putting her hands to her head.

questions.prompt: How did the mistake happen? Is anyone to blame: Anne, Marilla, Diana or no one?
facilitatorNotes: Marilla put the cordial in the cellar, not where she told Anne, and the currant wine was on the shelf. Anne never tasted it, so she could not know. Marilla blames Diana’s greed and says Anne is not to blame. A defensible answer is that it was an accident with Marilla’s mistake at its root; some readers will say Anne should have noticed that the bottle was not where she was told.
evidence: Marilla recollected that she had put the bottle of raspberry cordial down in the cellar instead of in the pantry as she had told Anne
I can’t see as you were to blame although I’m sorry it happened so.

questions.prompt: How does the narrator explain Mrs. Barry’s refusal? Why does Anne’s speech, which would have moved Mrs. Lynde, make Mrs. Barry angrier?
facilitatorNotes: The narrator is fair to her (“To do her justice”): she honestly believes Anne meant harm and wants to protect Diana. But Anne’s “big words and dramatic gestures” sound to her like mockery. The same speech would have softened Mrs. Lynde, so the outcome depends on the listener as much as on Anne. The narrator still calls her reply cold and cruel.
evidence: To do her justice, she really believed Anne had made Diana drunk out of sheer malice prepense
She was suspicious of Anne’s big words and dramatic gestures and imagined that the child was making fun of her.
This speech, which would have softened good Mrs. Lynde’s heart in a twinkling

questions.prompt: Marilla defends Anne to Mrs. Barry, laughs about the story with Matthew, and then kisses Anne asleep. What do these three moments together show about her?
facilitatorNotes: She is fiercely loyal (“Of all the unreasonable women”), she sees the comedy, and she has come to love Anne, though she shows tenderness only when no one sees. “Unaccustomed softness” tells us this is new for her. Readers may contrast her with Mrs. Barry, whose concern for her own daughter makes her hard toward someone else’s child.
evidence: Of all the unreasonable women I ever saw she’s the worst.
an unaccustomed softness crept into her face
Then she bent down and kissed the flushed cheek on the pillow.
